entry.title: Exploring Proxmark3: My Notes on Setting Up an NFC Sniffer and Tag Analysis
entry.summary: Recently, I bought a Proxmark3 device to learn more about hardware-level NFC and RFID protocol analysis. I wanted to see how wireless signals are exchanged between tag readers and smart cards under the hood.
entry.content:
Recently, I bought a Proxmark3 device to learn more about hardware-level NFC and RFID protocol analysis. I wanted to see how wireless signals are exchanged between tag readers and smart cards under the hood.

To keep my host environment clean, I set up the Proxmark3 client inside a Docker container on Ubuntu 24.04. After flashing and verifying the device, I scanned a sample ISO 14443-A tag (MIFARE Classic 1K) to analyze its UID structure, manufacturer memory blocks, and security settings.

In this post, I want to share my notes, what I learned from testing the device, and how to run tag diagnostic commands using Proxmark3.

What I Learned About Proxmark3 and NFC Tag Analysis​

When I first unboxed the Proxmark3, it looked like a simple circuit board with dual antennas. However, reading the hardware documentation and executing diagnostic commands revealed how powerful it is:

  1. Dockerized Environment Setup: Running the Proxmark3 client inside a Docker container allows seamless device mapping over USB serial (/dev/ttyACM0) without polluting the host operating system with build dependencies.
  2. Antenna Tuning: Using hw tune measures the power output in millivolts across both High Frequency (HF 13.56 MHz) and Low Frequency (LF 125 kHz) antennas to confirm optimal signal quality.
  3. ISO 14443-A Anticollision Handshake: Commands like hf search capture the low-level handshake parameters (ATQA 00 04, SAK 08, and 4-byte UID CF 6A 8F 6C) sent during initial card selection.
  4. Block 0 Manufacturer Data Structure: Sector 0 Block 0 contains the card UID, a Block Check Character (BCC) XOR checksum, and factory batch metadata.
  5. Static PRNG Security Risks: Running hf mf info detects pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) behavior. Finding a static nonce (01200145) indicates a weak clone chip or Chinese Magic Tag vulnerable to key recovery attacks.

Testing and Walkthrough​

Here are the practical steps I followed to set up the device, launch the client shell, and inspect the tag.

Step 1: Connecting Device and Launching Docker Shell​

After connecting the Proxmark3 via USB, I launched the containerized client using the ./pm3-docker.sh wrapper script. This script opens an interactive terminal connected directly to the Proxmark3 hardware.

Step 2: Hardware Verification and High-Frequency Tag Scanning​

Inside the Proxmark3 prompt, I ran hw version to confirm the client version and hardware memory. Then, I placed the test card on the antenna and ran hf search to detect ISO 14443-A signaling. Finally, running hf mf info printed detailed sector key information and PRNG status.

How Block 0 and Tag Security Work (Architecture)​

MIFARE Classic 1K tags organize memory into 16 sectors, with each sector containing 4 memory blocks of 16 bytes each.

1. Block 0 (Manufacturer Block) Anatomy​

Block 0 in Sector 0 stores critical identity data written during card manufacturing:

+----------------+----+-------+---------+---------------------------------+
| UID (4 bytes)  |BCC | SAK   |  ATQA   | Manufacturer Data (8 bytes)     |
+----------------+----+-------+---------+---------------------------------+
| CF 6A 8F 6C    | 46 |  08   |  04 00  | 62 63 91 8E 6D D4 68 69         |
+----------------+----+-------+---------+---------------------------------+

Field calculation breakdown:

  • UID (CF 6A 8F 6C): 4-byte single-size fixed identifier.
  • BCC (46): Block Check Character calculated by XOR-ing all 4 UID bytes (CF XOR 6A XOR 8F XOR 6C = 46).
  • SAK (08): Select Acknowledge byte confirming MIFARE Classic 1K architecture.
  • ATQA (04 00): Answer To Request byte in little-endian format.

2. PRNG Behavior and Tag Classification​

When authenticating, standard NXP chips generate a dynamic 32-bit random nonce. If a tag repeatedly responds with a fixed static nonce (01200145), it exposes the tag to static nested authentication exploits.

+---------------------------+
| ISO 14443-A Tag Detected  |
+-------------+-------------+
              |
              v
+---------------------------+
| ATQA: 00 04 / SAK: 08     |
+-------------+-------------+
              |
              v
+---------------------------+
| MIFARE Classic 1K Arch    |
+-------------+-------------+
              |
      +-------+-------+
      |               |
      v               v
Static Nonce    Random Nonce
 (01200145)           |
      |               v
      v         Genuine NXP IC
 Magic / Clone Tag

Docker Setup and PM3 Commands​

Here are the complete commands I used to build the Docker image, flash firmware, and test tags.

1. Docker Build and Launch Commands​

# Clone the official Proxmark3 repository
git clone https://github.com/RfidResearchGroup/proxmark3.git
cd proxmark3

# Set generic hardware target platform
echo "PLATFORM=PM3GENERIC" > Makefile.platform

# Build Docker image using Ubuntu 24.04 dockerfile
docker build -t pm3-ubuntu-24.04:1.0 -f docker/ubuntu-24.04/Dockerfile .

# Start interactive Proxmark3 client shell
./pm3-docker.sh

# Flash updated firmware images if needed
./pm3-docker.sh pm3-flash-all

2. Docker Launcher Wrapper Script (pm3-docker.sh)​

To simplify running the Proxmark3 client with automatic USB device mapping (/dev/ttyACM0) and X11 display forwarding, I used the following helper script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Helper script to run Proxmark3 client / flasher inside Docker container

IMAGE_NAME="pm3-ubuntu-24.04:1.0"
HOST_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"

# Detect serial devices
DEV_ARGS=()
if [ -c "/dev/ttyACM0" ]; then
    DEV_ARGS+=(--device=/dev/ttyACM0)
fi
for dev in /dev/pm3-*; do
    if [ -c "$dev" ]; then
        DEV_ARGS+=(--device="$dev")
    fi
done

# Pass X11 display if available for GUI plot window
DISPLAY_ARGS=()
if [ -n "$DISPLAY" ]; then
    DISPLAY_ARGS=(-e DISPLAY="$DISPLAY" -v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix)
fi

CMD=("./pm3")
if [ "$#" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -f "$1" ]; then
        CMD=("./$1" "${@:2}")
    elif [[ "$1" == "./"* ]]; then
        CMD=("$@")
    else
        CMD=("./pm3" "$@")
    fi
fi

exec docker run \
    --user $(id -u):$(id -g) \
    -e HOME=/tmp \
    --net=host \
    --privileged \
    "${DEV_ARGS[@]}" \
    "${DISPLAY_ARGS[@]}" \
    --volume="$HOST_DIR:/home/rrg/proxmark3" \
    -w /home/rrg/proxmark3 \
    --rm -it \
    "$IMAGE_NAME" "${CMD[@]}"

3. Essential PM3 Testing Commands​

CommandDescriptionCommand-Line Example
hw versionDisplay hardware, firmware, and flash memory details./pm3-docker.sh -c "hw version; exit"
hw tuneMeasure LF and HF antenna power output in millivolts./pm3-docker.sh -c "hw tune"
autoAutomatically scan and detect any RFID/NFC tag./pm3-docker.sh -c "auto"
hf searchScan for High Frequency 13.56 MHz ISO 14443-A/B tags./pm3-docker.sh -c "hf search"
hf mf infoAnalyze MIFARE Classic keys, sectors, and PRNG state./pm3-docker.sh -c "hf mf info"

Summary and Next Steps​

Setting up and testing the Proxmark3 gave me a clear, practical look at NFC hardware communication and tag security. Understanding parameter handshakes like ATQA, SAK, and PRNG nonces makes protocol debugging much easier.

References​

  • RfidResearchGroup Proxmark3 Official Repository

entry.title: Exploring AOSP MD Launcher: My Notes on Building and Multi-Display in Android
entry.summary: Recently, I have been learning about Android system internals. I wanted to understand how Android opens apps on different screens. This topic is very useful for car screens, foldables, and desktop modes.
entry.content:
Recently, I have been learning about Android system internals. I wanted to understand how Android opens apps on different screens. This topic is very useful for car screens, foldables, and desktop modes.

To learn how it works under the hood, I built and tested MD Launcher (MultiDisplay Launcher). It is an official sample app in the Android Open Source Project (development/samples/MultiDisplay).

In this post, I want to share my notes, what I learned from the code, and how I ran it on an emulator.

What I Learned About MD Launcher​

At first, MD Launcher looks like a simple home screen. But when I read the source code, I found several important features:

  1. Target Display Picker: You can select any connected screen from a dropdown menu. The app uses ActivityOptions.setLaunchDisplayId(displayId) to open new apps on that screen.
  2. Multi-Instance Launching: It has a checkbox to add FLAG_ACTIVITY_MULTIPLE_TASK with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK. This allows running the same app on two screens at the same time.
  3. Secondary Home Category: In AndroidManifest.xml, it uses both android.intent.category.HOME and android.intent.category.SECONDARY_HOME. This lets Android use it as the main home screen for external monitors.
  4. App Pinning: Users can pin app shortcuts onto the main home screen using a simple picker dialog.
  5. Display-Aware Live Wallpaper: The sample wallpaper engine (SampleWallpaper) uses getDisplayContext() to check screen density (densityDpi) whenever screen settings change.
  6. App Drawer Animation: It uses ViewAnimationUtils.createCircularReveal to show a smooth circular animation when opening the app drawer.

Testing on Android Emulator​

To test MD Launcher, I created a secondary display inside the Android Studio Emulator.

Step 1: Setting Up the Second Display​

  1. Start the Android Emulator.
  2. Open Extended Controls (...) > Displays.
  3. Click Add secondary display (1080p or 720p).

Step 2: Exploring the Launcher and Selecting a Display​

When MD Launcher opens on the main screen, it shows the pinned app icons and the display selector at the top. Tapping the bottom button opens the app drawer with all installed apps. Opening the display dropdown shows all connected screens, where I selected Display 2 (the new second screen).

Step 3: Opening Apps on the Second Screen​

With Display 2 selected, tapping an app (like Settings) opens it directly on the second screen.

How the App Works (Architecture)​

MD Launcher uses the standard MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel) pattern with Android Jetpack.

                    +-----------------------+
                    |   LauncherActivity    |
                    +-----------+-----------+
                                |
        +-----------------------+-----------------------+
        |                                               |
+-------v-------------------+               +-----------v---------------+
|     AppListViewModel      |               |  PinnedAppListViewModel   |
+---------------+-----------+               +-----------+---------------+
                |                                       |
    +-----------v-----------+               +-----------v---------------+
    | PackageIntentReceiver |               | SharedPreferences Listener|
    +-----------------------+               +---------------------------+

1. Activity Lifecycle and Launch Options​

In LauncherActivity.java:

  • It uses android:launchMode="singleTop" so the activity is not recreated when screens change.
  • Key code for opening apps on a target screen: 
    void launch(Intent launchIntent) {
        launchIntent.addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK);
        if (mNewInstanceCheckBox.isChecked()) {
            launchIntent.addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_MULTIPLE_TASK);
        }
        final ActivityOptions options = ActivityOptions.makeBasic();
        if (mSelectedDisplayId != Display.INVALID_DISPLAY) {
            options.setLaunchDisplayId(mSelectedDisplayId); // Open on target screen
        }
        startActivity(launchIntent, options.toBundle());
    }

2. Getting the App List (AppListViewModel)​

In AppListViewModel.java:

  • It gets the list of installed apps asynchronously using PackageManager.queryIntentActivities().
  • It uses PackageIntentReceiver to refresh the list automatically when a new app is installed or removed.

3. Saving Pinned Apps (PinnedAppListViewModel)​

In PinnedAppListViewModel.java:

  • It saves pinned apps in SharedPreferences and updates the screen when saved apps change.

Building and Installing​

MD Launcher is configured with Android's Soong build system using Android.bp.

Module Definition (Android.bp)​

android_app {
    name: "MultiDisplay",
    srcs: ["src/**/*.java"],
    static_libs: [
        "com.google.android.material_material",
        "androidx.lifecycle_lifecycle-livedata",
        "androidx.lifecycle_lifecycle-viewmodel",
    ],
    sdk_version: "current",
}

Build Commands​

source build/envsetup.sh
lunch aosp_car_x86_64-userdebug
make MultiDisplay

Install Command​

adb install -r $OUT/system/app/MultiDisplay/MultiDisplay.apk

Summary and Next Steps​

Building and testing MD Launcher helped me understand how Android handles multi-display features. The main key is using ActivityOptions.setLaunchDisplayId() to open apps on specific screens.

I am continuing to learn AOSP internals, system services, and multi-display development.

References​

  • AOSP MultiDisplay Sample Source Code
